newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK trade stuck in doldrums in 97 and 98.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK trade stuck in doldrums in 97 and 98.

text.p: Britain's international trade balance will ease further into the red in 1997 and 1998, as strong domestic growth and sterling's recent impressive rally dampen exports, Reuters quarterly poll of economic forecasts showed on Monday.
"It's down to lots of domestic demand and manufacturing getting hammered by a strong currency," said Paul Mortimer-Lee, chief capital markets economist at Paribas.

The trade deficit was forecast to dip to 13.8 billion sterling from a predicted average 12.0 billion sterling in 1996. The forecasts from 28 economists for trade in goods ranged from a massive 19.9 billion sterling deficit to a more optimistic 6.1 billion deficit for this year.
In quarter three 1996 Britain's trade in goods gap was 2.928 billion sterling.

The average prediction of a wide range of forecasts for Britain's current account -- the trade balance plus net earnings in invisible trade -- pointed to a worsening in 1997 to 4.8 billion sterling from 1.4 billion sterling in 1996. The current account deficit for the third quarter of last year was 71 million sterling.

Reuters poll, which was carried out between January 6 and 8, asked economists for quarterly predictions up to the third quarter of 1998. Added together, the average predictions for the first three quarters of that year suggest a further worsening in the visible trade and current account deficits to 12.4 billion sterling and 4.8 billion respectively.
Strong domestic demand would fuel imports, economists said.

"We're seeing stronger growth in the UK economy than in foreign economies and so this will make the UK market a target for foreign exporters...and will lead to some deterioration in the UK trade in goods position, said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking.

Sterling has recently traded around its highest levels for four years against the dollar and mark, and while the near term effects of this would boost the value of exports, higher prices would eventually dampen demand, economists said.
"There will be an impact on volumes...We export less and import more and that feeds through to a worse trade deficit," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

But the poll showed that sterling is unlikely to maintain its dizzy heights, softening to 2.5974 marks and 1.6673 dollars by the end of quarter one 1997. On January 8 when the poll closed, sterling ended at 2.6590 marks and 1.6875 dollars.
The average forecasts predict sterling weakening to 2.4244 marks and 1.5926 dollars by the end of 1998.
But the currency softening could be 'too little too late' for British manufacturers.
"What happens today will have a negative impact on competitiveness for some time," said Mortimer-Lee at Paribas.
